story.title: US Missionary Kevin Rideout Released After Kidnapping in Niger
story.summary: Kevin Rideout, an American missionary kidnapped in Niger last October, has been released after nine months in captivity. He is reported to be in good health and is currently in the care of US officials. His organization, SIM International, stated that he would soon be reunited with his family.

explore_lenses.label: Who is affected by the release?
explore_lenses.title: Rideout’s family and SIM are central
explore_lenses.summary: Kevin Rideout’s release directly affects his wife, children, extended family and SIM International colleagues after more than nine months apart. The organization says he is now with U.S. officials and asks that the family’s privacy be respected.

claims.text: SIM International says Rideout was taken from outside his home in Niamey on October 21, 2025, and was released after more than nine months in captivity.
SIM International says Rideout is in good health and in the care of U.S. officials.
Forecast (SIM International): Rideout will soon be reunited with his wife Krista, his children and extended family.
SIM International has asked the public to respect the family’s privacy while they reconnect.

explore_lenses.label: What does the evidence establish?
explore_lenses.title: Release is confirmed; circumstances are not
explore_lenses.summary: SIM International publicly confirmed the release, and CBS/AP reported the same account. Available reporting does not establish how he was freed or identify those responsible for the abduction.

claims.text: SIM International publicly confirmed Rideout’s release and stated that he is with U.S. officials; CBS News independently reported the organization’s statement.
Contemporaneous reporting said three armed people abducted Rideout in Niamey on October 21, 2025, and that he was likely driven out of the city.
No armed group publicly claimed responsibility for the kidnapping.
CBS News reported there was no initial public explanation for what led to the release.

explore_lenses.label: Why was a kidnapping risk flagged in Niger?
explore_lenses.title: U.S. warnings cover Niamey as well
explore_lenses.summary: Rideout’s abduction occurred amid an official U.S. assessment that Niger carries serious kidnapping, terrorism, crime and unrest risks. The State Department’s warning explicitly includes the capital, Niamey, not only remote border areas.

claims.text: The U.S. State Department lists Niger at Level 4, “Do Not Travel,” citing crime, unrest, terrorism, health risks, and kidnapping or hostage taking.

The State Department’s Niger advisory says terrorists use kidnapping for ransom and notes that a U.S. citizen was kidnapped from his home in Niamey in October 2025; it says criminal actors are suspected.
After Rideout’s abduction, the U.S. Embassy in Niamey warned that Americans faced a heightened kidnapping risk throughout Niger, including in the capital.
The State Department ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and eligible family members to leave Niger on January 30, 2026, citing safety risks.

story_report.summary: American missionary Kevin Rideout has been released after being held for more than nine months following his October 2025 kidnapping in Niger. His organization, SIM International, said he is in good health and in the care of U.S. officials. SIM said Rideout is expected to reunite soon with his wife, Krista, their children and extended family, while asking the public to respect the family’s privacy as they reconnect.

sections.heading: Rideout Abduction in Niamey
sections.body: SIM International said Rideout was taken from outside his home in Niamey on Oct. 21, 2025. Contemporaneous reporting said three armed people carried out the abduction and that he was likely driven out of the city. No armed group publicly claimed responsibility for the kidnapping.

sections.heading: Niger Kidnapping Risks for Americans
sections.body: The U.S. State Department lists Niger at Level 4, advising Americans not to travel because of crime, unrest, terrorism, health risks and kidnapping or hostage taking. Its advisory says terrorists use kidnapping for ransom and cites the October 2025 abduction of a U.S. citizen from a Niamey home, with criminal actors suspected. The U.S. Embassy in Niamey warned after the abduction of heightened kidnapping risk across the country, including the capital; the department later ordered non-emergency government employees and eligible family members to leave Niger.

related_stories.title: Ebola Outbreak in DRC Expands to Sixth Province Amid Rising Death Toll
related_stories.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now spread to a sixth province, Bas-Uele, following the death of a man who traveled from Haut-Uele. The World Health Organization has indicated that this outbreak is on track to become the deadliest in history, surpassing the previous record of over 11,000 fatalities from a decade ago. Currently, more than 2,100 deaths have been reported out of over 4,500 cases.

related_stories.title: USS George Washington Deploys to Middle East Amid Concerns Over USS Lincoln's Conditions
related_stories.summary: The USS George Washington aircraft carrier is en route to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has faced reports of declining mental health and supply issues among its crew during its record 260-day deployment. Some sailors aboard the Lincoln have reportedly attempted self-harm due to the conditions. However, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed these reports, calling them misrepresented, and senators are calling for an investigation into the situation.

related_stories.title: Zambians Vote in Presidential Election Amid Economic Concerns
related_stories.summary: Zambians voted on Thursday in a presidential election that tests the economic reforms of incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema. Approximately 8 million registered voters also selected members of Parliament and local councilors. Vote counting is currently underway, with results expected on Monday.
